set1.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with: left ventricular hypertrophy, right ventricular hypertrophy
set1.q: A 70-year-old woman has this electrocardiogram. Her S wave in V2 is 30 millimeters and her R wave in V5 is 19 millimeters (normal sum under 35). Which finding does it show?
opts: Right ventricular hypertrophy
Right ventricular hypertrophy shows more R than S wave in V1 and V2. These are deep S waves with tall lateral R waves.
Right bundle branch block
Right bundle branch block is a wide-QRS rSR pattern in V1. The finding here is voltage.
Left atrial enlargement
Left atrial enlargement is a P wave finding. The criterion met here is a QRS voltage sum.
Left ventricular hypertrophy
Correct. The deeper S wave in V1 or V2 added to the taller R wave in V5 or V6 is 49 millimeters, at least 35: left ventricular hypertrophy.

set1.io: Determine the electrical axis of an electrocardiogram
set1.q: A 64-year-old woman's limb leads are being read for a posterior fascicular block. Which lead has no significance in identifying it?
opts: Lead I
Lead I matters: it is mostly negative in left posterior fascicular block, with an r wave.
Lead III
Lead III matters: it is mostly positive, with a q wave, in left posterior fascicular block.
Lead II
Correct. Lead II has no significance in identifying left posterior fascicular block; it is usually positive or biphasic.
Lead aVF
aVF matters: it is mostly positive, which with a negative lead I gives right axis deviation.

set1.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with bundle branch blocks: right bundle branch block, left bundle branch block
set1.q: A 74-year-old man has this electrocardiogram. Which conduction abnormality does it show?
opts: Right bundle branch block
Correct. The QRS is wide, V1 shows an rSR pattern ending in a positive deflection, and the lateral leads carry slurred S waves: right bundle branch block.
Left bundle branch block
Left bundle branch block makes V1 end negative and notches the lateral leads without slurred S waves.
Left anterior fascicular block
Left anterior fascicular block is a narrow-QRS block with left axis deviation. These complexes are wide.
Left ventricular hypertrophy
Left ventricular hypertrophy raises voltage with a normal duration. These complexes are wide with an rSR in V1.

set1.io: Define: normal axis, left axis deviation, right axis deviation
set1.q: A 6-year-old boy has right axis deviation on a preoperative electrocardiogram. How should it be read?
opts: It always signals heart disease
Right axis deviation is listed as a normal finding in children, so in a child it does not by itself signal disease.
It means a left fascicle is blocked
A left posterior fascicular block can cause right axis deviation, but in a child the axis can simply be normal.
It can be normal in children
Correct. Right axis deviation is listed as normal in children.
It is caused by lead misplacement
Reversed arm leads can cause it, but right axis deviation is also a normal finding in children.

set1.io: Determine the electrical axis of an electrocardiogram
set1.q: A 61-year-old woman's 12-lead has a good general impression and standard calibration. What is assessed next?
opts: The axis
Correct. The systematic approach runs: general impression, calibration, axis, QRS assessment, hypertrophy and chamber enlargement, then ST and T wave changes.
The ST segments
ST and T wave changes come last in the systematic approach, after axis, QRS and hypertrophy.
Hypertrophy
Hypertrophy and chamber enlargement come after the axis and the QRS assessment.
Bundle branch blocks
Bundle branch blocks belong to the QRS assessment, which follows the axis.

set1.io: Determine the electrical axis of an electrocardiogram
set1.q: A 57-year-old woman has this electrocardiogram. What is her electrical axis?
opts: Normal axis
A normal axis has a mostly positive QRS in both lead I and aVF; the normal range is -30 to +90 degrees. That is not the pattern in leads I and aVF here.
Right axis deviation
Right axis deviation has lead I mostly negative and aVF mostly positive, an axis beyond +90 degrees. That is not the pattern in leads I and aVF here.
Extreme axis deviation
Extreme axis deviation, no man's land, has both lead I and aVF mostly negative. That is not the pattern in leads I and aVF here.
Left axis deviation
Correct. Lead I is mostly positive (up) and aVF is mostly negative (down): left axis deviation.

set1.io: Define: normal axis, left axis deviation, right axis deviation
set1.q: A 71-year-old man's QRS is mostly negative in both lead I and aVF. Which axis is this?
opts: Normal axis
A normal axis has a mostly positive QRS in both lead I and aVF; the normal range is -30 to +90 degrees. Here both are negative.
Extreme axis deviation
Correct. Both lead I and aVF mostly negative is extreme axis deviation, the region called no man's land.
Left axis deviation
Left axis deviation has lead I mostly positive and aVF mostly negative, an axis beyond -30 degrees. Here lead I is negative too.
Right axis deviation
Right axis deviation has lead I mostly negative and aVF mostly positive, an axis beyond +90 degrees. Here aVF is negative too.

set1.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with atrial enlargement
set1.q: A 66-year-old man's V1 shows a biphasic P wave with a small positive first part and a large negative second part. What does it indicate?
opts: Right atrial enlargement
Right atrial enlargement is the reverse in V1: the positive first part is the larger one.
Left atrial enlargement
Correct. A biphasic P wave in V1 with a small positive initial deflection and a large negative terminal deflection is left atrial enlargement.
Right ventricular hypertrophy
Right ventricular hypertrophy is a QRS finding, more R wave than S wave in V1 and V2.
Left ventricular hypertrophy
Left ventricular hypertrophy is a QRS voltage finding, not a biphasic P wave in V1.

set1.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with: left ventricular hypertrophy, right ventricular hypertrophy
set1.q: A 23-year-old woman has this electrocardiogram. Which finding does it show?
opts: Left ventricular hypertrophy
Left ventricular hypertrophy puts deep S waves in V1 and V2 and can cause left axis deviation. Here V1 is dominantly positive.
Right ventricular hypertrophy
Correct. Tall R waves exceeding the S waves in V1 and V2, with right axis deviation (lead I negative): right ventricular hypertrophy.
Left bundle branch block
Left bundle branch block makes V1 end negative with a wide QRS. V1 here is a tall positive complex.
Right atrial enlargement
Right atrial enlargement is a P wave finding. The main change on this tracing is the tall R wave in V1.

set1.io: Determine the electrical axis of an electrocardiogram
set1.q: A 52-year-old woman has this electrocardiogram. What is her electrical axis?
opts: Normal axis
A normal axis has a mostly positive QRS in both lead I and aVF; the normal range is -30 to +90 degrees. That is not the pattern in leads I and aVF here.
Left axis deviation
Left axis deviation has lead I mostly positive and aVF mostly negative, an axis beyond -30 degrees. That is not the pattern in leads I and aVF here.
Right axis deviation
Correct. Lead I is mostly negative and aVF mostly positive: right axis deviation, here alongside peaked P waves.
Extreme axis deviation
Extreme axis deviation, no man's land, has both lead I and aVF mostly negative. That is not the pattern in leads I and aVF here.

set1.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with atrial enlargement: left atrial enlargement, right atrial enlargement
set1.q: A 70-year-old man has this lead II strip. Which chamber finding do its P waves show?
opts: Right atrial enlargement
Right atrial enlargement gives tall, peaked P waves. These are wide and double-humped.
Right ventricular hypertrophy
Right ventricular hypertrophy is read from the QRS in V1 and V2. The finding here is the P wave.
Left atrial enlargement
Correct. The P waves are wide and humped with the humps well apart: P mitrale, left atrial enlargement.
Left ventricular hypertrophy
Left ventricular hypertrophy is a QRS voltage finding. The finding here is the P wave.

set1.io: Define: normal axis, left axis deviation, right axis deviation
set1.q: A 59-year-old woman's axis lies beyond -30 degrees (normal -30 to +90). Which category is this?
opts: Left axis deviation
Correct. Beyond -30 degrees, toward -90, is left axis deviation; the normal range ends at -30 degrees.
Normal axis
The normal axis stops at -30 degrees. An axis beyond -30 has deviated to the left.
Right axis deviation
Right axis deviation lies beyond +90 degrees, on the opposite side of the circle.
Extreme axis deviation
Extreme axis deviation lies between -90 and 180 degrees, where both lead I and aVF are negative.

set1.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with atrial enlargement: left atrial enlargement, right atrial enlargement
set1.q: A 59-year-old woman with pulmonary hypertension has this lead II strip. Her P waves are taller than 2.5 millimeters (normal 2.5 or less). What do they indicate?
opts: Left atrial enlargement
Left atrial enlargement widens and notches the P wave rather than making it tall and peaked.
Right ventricular hypertrophy
Right ventricular hypertrophy is a QRS finding in V1 and V2, not a P wave height in lead II.
Left ventricular hypertrophy
Left ventricular hypertrophy raises QRS voltage; it does not make the P wave tall.
Right atrial enlargement
Correct. An upright limb-lead P wave taller than 2.5 millimeters is P pulmonale, and one lead is enough to confirm right atrial enlargement.

set1.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with bundle branch blocks: right bundle branch block, left bundle branch block
set1.q: A 73-year-old woman has this electrocardiogram. Tracing back from the J point in V1, what is the first deflection you reach?
opts: A positive deflection
A positive first deflection back from the J point in V1 is the rule for right bundle branch block. This V1 ends negative.
A flat, isoelectric segment
The QRS in V1 here is a deep negative complex; tracing back from the J point lands on it, not on a flat segment.
A pacer spike
There are no pacer spikes on this tracing. The first deflection back from the J point in V1 is negative.
A negative deflection
Correct. In left bundle branch block, the first deflection you come to traveling back from the J point in V1 is negative (an rS pattern).

set1.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with atrial enlargement
set1.q: A 57-year-old man's V1 shows a biphasic P wave with a larger positive first part and a smaller negative second part. What does it indicate?
opts: Left atrial enlargement
Left atrial enlargement is the reverse in V1: a small positive start and a large negative terminal deflection.
Right ventricular hypertrophy
Right ventricular hypertrophy is a QRS finding in V1 and V2, not a biphasic P wave.
Left ventricular hypertrophy
Left ventricular hypertrophy raises QRS voltage; it does not shape the P wave in V1.
Right atrial enlargement
Correct. A biphasic P wave in V1 with a larger positive initial deflection and a smaller negative terminal deflection is right atrial enlargement.

set1.io: Discuss related anatomy and physiology of ventricular conduction abnormalities and chamber enlargement
set1.q: A 75-year-old woman has left bundle branch block. Which ventricle depolarizes first?
opts: The right ventricle
Correct. Impulses travel down the right bundle normally, so the right ventricle contracts first; the left must wait for myocyte-to-myocyte spread.
The left ventricle
The left bundle is the blocked one, so the left ventricle depolarizes late, after the impulse crosses from the right.
Both at the same time
Simultaneous depolarization is normal conduction. In a bundle branch block the ventricles contract in sequence.
The septum, left to right
Normal septal depolarization runs left to right, but in left bundle branch block the septal fascicle is blocked too.

set1.io: Determine the electrical axis of an electrocardiogram
set1.q: A 70-year-old woman has these limb leads with a narrow QRS. Which conduction abnormality do they show?
opts: Left anterior fascicular block
Left anterior fascicular block gives left axis deviation, lead I positive and aVF negative. Here lead I is negative.
Left bundle branch block
Left bundle branch block is a wide-QRS block. These complexes are narrow.
Right bundle branch block
Right bundle branch block is wide, with an rSR pattern in V1. These complexes are narrow.
Left posterior fascicular block
Correct. Right axis deviation (lead I mostly negative, aVF positive), an r wave in lead I with a q wave in lead III, and a positive lead III: left posterior fascicular block.

set1.io: Discuss related anatomy and physiology of ventricular conduction abnormalities and chamber enlargement
set1.q: A 72-year-old man with long-standing lung disease has right axis deviation. Which is a listed cause?
opts: Left anterior fascicular block
Left anterior fascicular block produces left axis deviation, lead I up and aVF down.
Past inferior infarction
A past inferior infarction is a cause of left axis deviation.
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
Correct. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is a cause of right axis deviation; lung disease makes the right heart work harder.
Tricuspid atresia
Tricuspid atresia is listed among the causes of left axis deviation, not right.

set1.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with ventricular hypertrophy
set1.q: A 68-year-old man has more R wave than S wave in V1 and V2. Which finding makes that criterion unreliable for right ventricular hypertrophy?
opts: Right bundle branch block
Correct. Right bundle branch block, posterior wall infarction and age under 7 or 8 also give a tall R wave in V1, so the criterion is unreliable with them.
Right axis deviation
Right axis deviation is a supportive criterion for right ventricular hypertrophy, not a reason to distrust the R wave.
Right atrial enlargement
Right atrial enlargement supports right ventricular hypertrophy rather than making the R wave criterion unreliable.
A strain pattern in V1 and V2
A strain pattern supports right ventricular hypertrophy. Right bundle branch block is what makes the criterion unreliable.

set1.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with atrial enlargement: left atrial enlargement, right atrial enlargement
set1.q: A 65-year-old woman's lead II P wave is shown; it measures at least 0.12 seconds (normal under 0.12). What does it indicate?
opts: Right atrial enlargement
Right atrial enlargement makes the P wave tall and peaked, over 2.5 millimeters, rather than wide and notched.
Right ventricular hypertrophy
Right ventricular hypertrophy is a QRS finding in V1 and V2, not a notched P wave.
Left ventricular hypertrophy
Left ventricular hypertrophy is a QRS voltage finding; the change here is in the P wave.
Left atrial enlargement
Correct. An upright, humped P wave at least 0.12 seconds long with the humps at least 0.04 seconds apart is P mitrale: left atrial enlargement.
set1.alt: Drawn tracing of three cardiac cycles

set1.io: Define: normal axis, left axis deviation, right axis deviation
set1.q: A 48-year-old woman's lead I QRS is mostly negative and her aVF QRS is mostly positive. Which axis is this?
opts: Normal axis
A normal axis has a mostly positive QRS in both lead I and aVF; the normal range is -30 to +90 degrees. Here lead I is negative.
Right axis deviation
Correct. Lead I mostly negative with aVF mostly positive is right axis deviation.
Left axis deviation
Left axis deviation has lead I mostly positive and aVF mostly negative, an axis beyond -30 degrees. Here the pattern is reversed.
Extreme axis deviation
Extreme axis deviation, no man's land, has both lead I and aVF mostly negative. Here aVF is positive.

set1.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with bundle branch blocks: incomplete and complete right bundle branch block, incomplete and complete left bundle branch block
set1.q: A 77-year-old woman has a wide QRS with slurred S waves in leads I, aVL, V5 and V6. Which block is this?
opts: Right bundle branch block
Correct. Slurred S waves in the lateral leads are a right bundle branch block criterion, the double QRS phenomenon best seen in V6.
Left bundle branch block
Left bundle branch block notches the lateral QRS complexes and removes their Q waves; it does not give slurred S waves.
Left anterior fascicular block
A fascicular block keeps the QRS narrow and is diagnosed by axis and limb-lead patterns.
Left ventricular hypertrophy
Left ventricular hypertrophy gives tall lateral R waves with a normal duration, not slurred S waves.

set1.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with: left ventricular hypertrophy, right ventricular hypertrophy
set1.q: A 79-year-old man has this electrocardiogram. His R wave in aVL is 22 millimeters (normal 12 or less). Which finding does it show?
opts: Left ventricular hypertrophy
Correct. An R wave in aVL greater than 12 millimeters meets a criterion for left ventricular hypertrophy.
Right ventricular hypertrophy
Right ventricular hypertrophy is read from V1 and V2 (more R than S wave), not from a tall R wave in aVL.
Left anterior fascicular block
A fascicular block is an axis and limb-lead pattern with a normal voltage. The criterion met here is aVL voltage.
Right atrial enlargement
Right atrial enlargement is a P wave finding, not an R wave height.

set1.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with bundle branch blocks: right bundle branch block, left bundle branch block
set1.q: A 70-year-old woman has a bundle branch block. Which lead decides whether the block is right or left?
opts: Lead II
Lead II is the rhythm lead; the side of a bundle branch block is read in V1, by the first deflection before the J point.
aVR
aVR does not decide the side of the block; V1 does, through the direction of the deflection just before the J point.
V1
Correct. Find the J point in V1 and travel backward: if the first deflection you reach is positive the block is right-sided, and if it is negative the block is left-sided.
V4
V4 does not decide the side; V1 decides it, and V6 is where the double QRS phenomenon is best seen.

set1.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with atrial enlargement: left atrial enlargement, right atrial enlargement
set1.q: A 66-year-old man with emphysema has these limb leads. Which chamber finding do they show?
opts: Left atrial enlargement
Left atrial enlargement makes the limb-lead P wave wide and humped, at least 0.12 seconds, not tall and peaked.
Right atrial enlargement
Correct. Tall, peaked, upright P waves in the limb leads, taller than 2.5 millimeters, are P pulmonale: right atrial enlargement.
Right ventricular hypertrophy
Right ventricular hypertrophy is read from V1 and V2 (more R wave than S wave). These limb leads show a P wave change.
Left ventricular hypertrophy
Left ventricular hypertrophy is a QRS voltage finding. The striking change here is in the P waves.

set1.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with: left ventricular hypertrophy, right ventricular hypertrophy
set1.q: A 45-year-old woman with pulmonary hypertension has this electrocardiogram. Which finding does it show?
opts: Left ventricular hypertrophy
Left ventricular hypertrophy gives deep S waves in V1 and V2 with tall lateral R waves. V1 here is dominantly positive.
Right bundle branch block
Right bundle branch block also gives a tall R wave in V1, but it needs a QRS of 0.12 seconds or longer with an rSR in V1; here the tall R comes with strain and right axis deviation.
Right ventricular hypertrophy
Correct. More R wave than S wave in V1 and V2, a strain pattern there, right axis deviation and right atrial enlargement: right ventricular hypertrophy.
Left atrial enlargement
Left atrial enlargement is a P wave finding (P mitrale). The striking change here is in the QRS of V1 and V2.

set1.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with bundle branch blocks: right bundle branch block, left bundle branch block
set1.q: A 78-year-old man has this electrocardiogram. What do its lateral leads (I, aVL, V5, V6) lack?
opts: R waves
The lateral leads in left bundle branch block have tall, often notched R waves. It is the Q wave that is missing.
Q waves
Correct. In left bundle branch block the septal fascicle is blocked, so the septum's normal Q wave is lost from the lateral leads.
T waves
T waves are present after each complex. The missing wave is the septal Q wave.
P waves
P waves are atrial and appear across the leads in sinus rhythm. The lateral leads lack Q waves.

set1.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with bundle branch blocks: right bundle branch block, left bundle branch block
set1.q: A 68-year-old woman has this electrocardiogram. Which conduction abnormality does it show?
opts: Right bundle branch block
Right bundle branch block ends V1 with a positive R wave. Here the last deflection before the J point in V1 is negative.
Left bundle branch block
Correct. The QRS is wide, V1 is an rS pattern ending negative, and the lateral leads are notched with no Q waves: left bundle branch block, here with left axis deviation.
Left anterior fascicular block
Left anterior fascicular block shares the left axis but keeps a narrow QRS. These complexes are wide.
Left atrial enlargement
Left atrial enlargement changes the P wave, not the width and shape of the QRS.

set1.io: Determine the electrical axis of an electrocardiogram
set1.q: A 58-year-old woman with lung disease has this electrocardiogram. What is her electrical axis?
opts: Right axis deviation
Correct. Lead I is mostly negative and aVF is mostly positive: right axis deviation.
Normal axis
A normal axis has a mostly positive QRS in both lead I and aVF; the normal range is -30 to +90 degrees. That is not the pattern in leads I and aVF here.
Left axis deviation
Left axis deviation has lead I mostly positive and aVF mostly negative, an axis beyond -30 degrees. That is not the pattern in leads I and aVF here.
Extreme axis deviation
Extreme axis deviation, no man's land, has both lead I and aVF mostly negative. That is not the pattern in leads I and aVF here.

set1.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with ventricular hypertrophy
set1.q: A 64-year-old woman has ST elevation that may not be an infarction. Which condition is the most common mimic of ST-elevation infarction?
opts: Right ventricular hypertrophy
Right ventricular hypertrophy is not on the list of infarction mimics; left ventricular hypertrophy is the most common mimic.
Left ventricular hypertrophy
Correct. Left ventricular hypertrophy is known as the most common mimic of ST-elevation myocardial infarction: it alters repolarization, changing the ST segment and T wave.
Right atrial enlargement
Right atrial enlargement is a P wave finding and does not mimic ST elevation.
Left anterior fascicular block
A fascicular block shifts the axis; it is not on the list of infarction mimics.

set2.io: Determine the electrical axis of an electrocardiogram
set2.q: A 70-year-old man has this electrocardiogram. What is his electrical axis?
opts: Normal axis
A normal axis has a mostly positive QRS in both lead I and aVF; the normal range is -30 to +90 degrees. That is not the pattern in leads I and aVF here.
Extreme axis deviation
Correct. Both lead I and aVF are mostly negative: extreme axis deviation, the region called no man's land.
Left axis deviation
Left axis deviation has lead I mostly positive and aVF mostly negative, an axis beyond -30 degrees. That is not the pattern in leads I and aVF here.
Right axis deviation
Right axis deviation has lead I mostly negative and aVF mostly positive, an axis beyond +90 degrees. That is not the pattern in leads I and aVF here.

set2.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with ventricular hypertrophy
set2.q: A 70-year-old man with hypertension has ST elevation in V1 to V3 on this electrocardiogram. Which condition explains the pattern as a mimic?
opts: Left ventricular hypertrophy
Correct. Huge QRS voltages with concave, upward-sloping ST elevation in V1 to V3 and lateral T wave inversion are left ventricular hypertrophy, the most common mimic of ST-elevation infarction.
Right ventricular hypertrophy
Right ventricular hypertrophy shows more R than S wave in V1 and V2 with a strain pattern. Here V1 to V3 are deep S waves with concave elevation.
Right bundle branch block
Right bundle branch block gives an rSR in V1 with slurred lateral S waves, not huge voltages with concave elevation.
Left atrial enlargement
Left atrial enlargement is a P wave finding and does not elevate the ST segment.

set2.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with: left ventricular hypertrophy, right ventricular hypertrophy
set2.q: A 54-year-old woman has this V1 complex. What does its ST segment and T wave show?
opts: A strain pattern
Correct. A strain pattern is the shape of the ST segment from the J point into an inverted, asymmetrical T wave, seen in V1 and V2.
Peaked P waves
Peaked P waves are right atrial enlargement, a P wave finding. The finding here is after the QRS.
Lateral notching
Notching is a QRS finding of left bundle branch block in the lateral leads. This is the ST and T wave in V1.
A normal T wave
A normal T wave is upright and symmetric. This one is inverted and asymmetric after a sloping ST segment.
set2.alt: One drawn complex on electrocardiogram paper

set2.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with: left ventricular hypertrophy, right ventricular hypertrophy
set2.q: A 69-year-old woman's chest leads are measured for left ventricular hypertrophy. Which single-lead finding meets a criterion?
opts: Any chest lead over 15 millimeters
Fifteen millimeters is far below the threshold. A single chest lead must exceed 45 millimeters.
Any chest lead over 45 millimeters
Correct. If any chest lead is greater than 45 millimeters, left ventricular hypertrophy is present.
Any limb lead over 25 millimeters
The single-lead limb criterion is aVL over 12 millimeters. The chest-lead criterion is any lead over 45.
A V1 R wave over 10 millimeters
A tall R in V1 suggests the right ventricle, not the left. Left ventricular hypertrophy uses any chest lead over 45.

set2.io: Determine the electrical axis of an electrocardiogram
set2.q: A 45-year-old woman has a routine electrocardiogram. What is her electrical axis?
opts: Left axis deviation
Left axis deviation has lead I mostly positive and aVF mostly negative, an axis beyond -30 degrees. That is not the pattern in leads I and aVF here.
Right axis deviation
Right axis deviation has lead I mostly negative and aVF mostly positive, an axis beyond +90 degrees. That is not the pattern in leads I and aVF here.
Normal axis
Correct. The QRS is mostly positive in both lead I and aVF, so the axis falls in the normal range of -30 to +90 degrees.
Extreme axis deviation
Extreme axis deviation, no man's land, has both lead I and aVF mostly negative. That is not the pattern in leads I and aVF here.

set2.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with bundle branch blocks: right bundle branch block, left bundle branch block
set2.q: A 74-year-old woman has this electrocardiogram. Which lateral-lead finding supports the diagnosis?
opts: Notched R waves
Notched lateral R waves without Q waves are the left bundle branch block pattern.
Slurred S waves
Correct. Right bundle branch block puts slurred S waves in the lateral leads (I, aVL, V5, V6), the double QRS phenomenon, best seen in V6.
Absent Q waves
Loss of lateral Q waves belongs to left bundle branch block, where the septal fascicle is blocked.
Tall peaked P waves
Tall peaked P waves in the limb leads are right atrial enlargement, not a bundle branch block finding.

set2.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with bundle branch blocks: right bundle branch block, left bundle branch block
set2.q: A 64-year-old man's QRS is 0.13 seconds (normal under 0.12). Which V1 pattern fits right bundle branch block?
opts: rS pattern
An rS pattern in V1, ending negative, is left bundle branch block.
QS pattern
A wholly negative complex in V1 ends negative, the left bundle branch block side.
Notched R in V6 only
A notched R in V6 is the left bundle branch block double QRS phenomenon, not a V1 pattern of the right side.
rSR pattern
Correct. Right bundle branch block shows an rSR pattern in V1, so the first deflection back from the J point is positive.

set2.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with bundle branch blocks: incomplete and complete right bundle branch block, incomplete and complete left bundle branch block
set2.q: A 75-year-old man has a wide QRS with notched lateral complexes and no Q waves in I, aVL, V5 and V6. Which block is this?
opts: Right bundle branch block
Right bundle branch block gives slurred lateral S waves and an rSR in V1, not notching with absent Q waves.
Left posterior fascicular block
A fascicular block keeps the QRS narrow and does not notch the lateral complexes.
Left bundle branch block
Correct. Notching of the lateral QRS complexes, the double QRS phenomenon best seen in V6, with no lateral Q waves is left bundle branch block.
Right ventricular hypertrophy
Right ventricular hypertrophy changes V1 and V2 (more R than S wave), not the lateral leads in this way.

set2.io: Define: normal axis, left axis deviation, right axis deviation
set2.q: A 50-year-old woman asks why her axis is assessed on every 12-lead. Which factors can shift the cardiac axis?
opts: Age, history and disease
Correct. A patient's age, medical history and disease processes, chronic or acute, can affect the axis of the heart.
Paper speed and calibration
Paper speed and calibration change how a tracing is drawn, not the direction of the mean electrical vector.
The P wave height and shape
The axis is the direction of the QRS vector. P waves are atrial and do not set it.
The PR interval duration
The PR interval reflects conduction through the atrioventricular node, not the direction of the QRS axis.

set2.io: Discuss related anatomy and physiology of ventricular conduction abnormalities and chamber enlargement
set2.q: A 62-year-old man develops a new intraventricular conduction abnormality. Which one is most common during an acute myocardial infarction?
opts: Left posterior fascicular block
Left posterior fascicular block is far less common than the anterior one.
Left bundle branch block
Left bundle branch block blocks all three fascicles at once. The single most common abnormality in acute infarction is the anterior fascicular block.
Right bundle branch block
Right bundle branch block can also appear during an acute infarction, but the most common intraventricular conduction abnormality there is left anterior fascicular block.
Left anterior fascicular block
Correct. Left anterior fascicular block, the left anterior hemiblock, is the most common intraventricular conduction abnormality during an acute myocardial infarction.

set2.io: Discuss related anatomy and physiology of ventricular conduction abnormalities and chamber enlargement
set2.q: A 58-year-old man is learning his conduction system. Into which three fascicles does the left bundle branch split?
opts: Anterior, posterior and right
The right bundle branch is a separate branch, not a fascicle of the left bundle. The third left fascicle is the septal one.
Superior, inferior and lateral
The left bundle's fascicles are named anterior, posterior and septal.
Anterior, posterior and septal
Correct. The left bundle arises from the His bundle and quickly splits into the posterior, anterior and interventricular septal fascicles.
Septal, apical and basal
There are no apical or basal fascicles. The left bundle splits into anterior, posterior and septal fascicles.

set2.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with bundle branch blocks: right bundle branch block, left bundle branch block
set2.q: A 72-year-old woman's QRS is 0.12 seconds or longer (normal under 0.12). Her V1 and V6 complexes are shown. Which block is this?
opts: Right bundle branch block
Right bundle branch block makes V1 an rSR pattern ending positive, with a slurred S wave in V6.
Left anterior fascicular block
A fascicular block keeps the QRS narrow. This QRS is 0.12 seconds or longer.
Right ventricular hypertrophy
Right ventricular hypertrophy puts more R wave than S wave in V1. This V1 is mostly a deep S wave.
Left bundle branch block
Correct. V1 is an rS pattern whose first deflection back from the J point is negative, and V6 is a notched R wave: left bundle branch block.
set2.alt: Two drawn complexes, leads V1 and V6

set2.io: Discuss related anatomy and physiology of ventricular conduction abnormalities and chamber enlargement
set2.q: A 66-year-old woman has ventricular hypertrophy. What does that term refer to?
opts: Stretching that dilates a chamber
Stretching and dilation is chamber enlargement, most often of the atria. Hypertrophy thickens the muscle.
A block in a bundle branch
A bundle branch block is a conduction problem, not a change in the muscle's thickness.
Thickening of the heart muscle

Correct. Ventricular hypertrophy is actual enlargement and thickening of the cardiac muscle; in pressure overload the thick wall can make the chamber smaller, but in volume overload the chamber dilates as well.
Thinning that enlarges a chamber
Hypertrophy thickens the wall rather than thinning it, so thinning with a larger chamber is not what the term means.

set2.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with bundle branch blocks: right bundle branch block, left bundle branch block
set2.q: A 67-year-old man's QRS is 0.12 seconds or longer (normal under 0.12). His V1 and V6 complexes are shown. Which block is this?
opts: Left bundle branch block
Left bundle branch block makes V1 an rS pattern ending negative, with a notched R in V6.
Left posterior fascicular block
A fascicular block keeps the QRS narrow. This QRS is 0.12 seconds or longer.
Left ventricular hypertrophy
Left ventricular hypertrophy gives deep S waves in V1 and tall lateral R waves at a normal duration.
Right bundle branch block
Correct. V1 is an rSR pattern whose first deflection back from the J point is positive, and V6 has a slurred S wave: right bundle branch block.
set2.alt: Two drawn complexes, leads V1 and V6

set2.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with: left ventricular hypertrophy, right ventricular hypertrophy
set2.q: A 66-year-old man with long-standing hypertension has this electrocardiogram. Which finding does it show?
opts: Left ventricular hypertrophy
Correct. Very deep S waves in V1 and V2 and tall R waves in V5 and V6, adding up well past 35 millimeters: left ventricular hypertrophy.
Right ventricular hypertrophy
Right ventricular hypertrophy puts more R wave than S wave in V1 and V2. Here V1 and V2 are deep S waves.
Left bundle branch block
Left bundle branch block needs a QRS of 0.12 seconds or longer. The striking change here is voltage, not width.
Right atrial enlargement
Right atrial enlargement is a P wave finding. The striking change here is QRS voltage.

set2.io: Discuss related anatomy and physiology of ventricular conduction abnormalities and chamber enlargement
set2.q: A 64-year-old man has a new wide-complex tachycardia with extreme axis deviation. Which rhythm does that axis raise suspicion for?
opts: Ventricular tachycardia
Correct. A ventricular arrhythmia is one of the causes of extreme axis deviation; a wide-complex tachycardia in no man's land points toward ventricular tachycardia.
Sinus tachycardia
Sinus tachycardia uses the normal pathway and leaves the axis normal. Extreme deviation suggests a ventricular origin.
Left anterior fascicular block
Left anterior fascicular block causes left axis deviation with a narrow QRS, not a wide tachycardia in no man's land.
Right atrial enlargement
Right atrial enlargement changes the P wave, not the QRS axis of a tachycardia.

set2.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with bundle branch blocks: right bundle branch block, left bundle branch block
set2.q: A 71-year-old man has this electrocardiogram. Which conduction abnormality does it show?
opts: Right bundle branch block
Right bundle branch block shows a positive deflection before the J point in V1 (rSR) and slurred lateral S waves. V1 here is negative.
Left bundle branch block
Correct. A wide QRS, a negative first deflection back from the J point in V1, notched lateral QRS complexes and no lateral Q waves: left bundle branch block.
Left anterior fascicular block
Left anterior fascicular block has a narrow QRS with left axis deviation. These complexes are wide.
Left ventricular hypertrophy
Hypertrophy raises voltage with a normal QRS duration. These complexes are wide, with lateral notching.

set2.io: Determine the electrical axis of an electrocardiogram
set2.q: A 36-year-old woman has this electrocardiogram. On a systematic read, how is her QRS assessed?
opts: Right bundle branch block
Right bundle branch block would widen the QRS to 0.12 seconds or longer with an rSR in V1. This QRS is narrow.
Within normal limits
Correct. The QRS is narrow, with no bundle branch or fascicular block pattern: within normal limits, with a normal axis and no enlargement.
Left bundle branch block
Left bundle branch block would widen the QRS and notch the lateral leads. This QRS is narrow.
Left anterior fascicular block
Left anterior fascicular block needs left axis deviation. This axis is normal: lead I and aVF are positive.

set2.io: Define: normal axis, left axis deviation, right axis deviation
set2.q: A 40-year-old man's electrocardiogram is reviewed for axis. Which range is the normal electrical axis?
opts: 0 to +180 degrees
That range would take in most of right axis deviation. The normal axis runs from -30 to +90 degrees.
-30 to +90 degrees
Correct. The normal electrical axis ranges between -30 and +90 degrees; both lead I and aVF are mostly positive.
+90 to +180 degrees
That is right axis deviation, where lead I turns negative and aVF stays positive.
-30 to -90 degrees
That is left axis deviation, where lead I is positive and aVF negative.

set2.io: Determine the electrical axis of an electrocardiogram
set2.q: A 66-year-old man has this electrocardiogram with a narrow QRS. Which conduction abnormality does it show?
opts: Left posterior fascicular block
Left posterior fascicular block gives right axis deviation, lead I negative and aVF positive. Here lead I is positive.
Left bundle branch block
Left bundle branch block needs a QRS of 0.12 seconds or longer. This QRS is narrow.
Right bundle branch block
Right bundle branch block needs a wide QRS with an rSR pattern in V1. This QRS is narrow.
Left anterior fascicular block
Correct. Left axis deviation (lead I up, aVF down), a q wave in lead I with an r wave in lead III, and mostly negative leads II and III with a narrow QRS: left anterior fascicular block.

set2.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with atrial enlargement: left atrial enlargement, right atrial enlargement
set2.q: A 52-year-old woman has this electrocardiogram with right axis deviation. Which chamber finding do its P waves show?
opts: Left atrial enlargement
Left atrial enlargement gives humped, wide limb-lead P waves and a large negative terminal P in V1. These P waves are tall and peaked.
Right ventricular hypertrophy
Right ventricular hypertrophy would show more R wave than S wave in V1 and V2. The finding here is in the P waves.
Left ventricular hypertrophy
Left ventricular hypertrophy is a QRS voltage finding with left axis deviation. This tracing has right axis deviation and peaked P waves.
Right atrial enlargement
Correct. The limb-lead P waves are tall and peaked and V1 shows a biphasic P with a larger positive first part: right atrial enlargement.

set2.io: Discuss related anatomy and physiology of ventricular conduction abnormalities and chamber enlargement
set2.q: A 72-year-old woman has a bundle branch block with a double-humped QRS. What produces this two-QRS-complex phenomenon?
opts: Ventricles depolarizing in sequence
Correct. Because the ventricles are contracted in sequence rather than at the same time, the QRS shows two humps: the two QRS complex phenomenon.
Two separate pacemakers firing
Two independent pacemakers describe third-degree block. In a bundle branch block one impulse reaches the ventricles at different times.
Atrial and ventricular overlap
The P wave is not fused into the QRS here. The two humps come from the two ventricles depolarizing one after the other.
A pacer spike before each QRS
A pacer spike is a device artifact. The double QRS comes from sequential ventricular depolarization.

set2.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with bundle branch blocks: incomplete and complete right bundle branch block, incomplete and complete left bundle branch block
set2.q: A 61-year-old woman is told her electrocardiogram shows bunny ears in V1. Why should that pattern not be relied on?
opts: Bunny ears mean left bundle block
Bunny ears are taught for the right side, and even there they are not reliable. The J point rule decides.
Bunny ears are a normal variant
The problem is not that bunny ears are normal; it is that right bundle branch block takes many V1 shapes besides them.
Bunny ears need a narrow QRS
Every bundle branch block has a wide QRS. The issue is that V1 morphology varies, while the J point rule does not.
Right bundle block has many V1 shapes
Correct. Right bundle branch block can have many morphologies in V1; the constant is that the first deflection back from the J point is positive.

set2.io: Determine the electrical axis of an electrocardiogram
set2.q: A 55-year-old woman's electrocardiogram needs a quick axis determination. Which two leads are used?
opts: Lead I and aVF
Correct. Leads I and aVF are used to quickly determine the axis: they sit at either end of the normal sector.
Leads II and III
Leads II and III add detail, but the quick method uses lead I and aVF.
Leads V1 and V6
V1 and V6 are precordial leads used for bundle branch block morphology, not for the frontal axis.
Leads aVR and aVL
The quick method uses lead I and aVF. aVR and aVL are not the pair it relies on.

set2.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with atrial enlargement: left atrial enlargement, right atrial enlargement
set2.q: A 68-year-old woman with mitral valve disease has this V1. What do its P waves show?
opts: Right atrial enlargement
Right atrial enlargement makes the V1 P wave's positive first part the larger one. Here the negative terminal part dominates.
Right ventricular hypertrophy
Right ventricular hypertrophy shows more R wave than S wave in V1. The marked finding here is the P wave.
Left atrial enlargement
Correct. A biphasic P wave in V1 with a small positive start and a large negative terminal deflection is P mitrale: left atrial enlargement.
Left ventricular hypertrophy
Left ventricular hypertrophy is a QRS voltage finding. The marked finding here is the P wave.
set2.alt: Lead V1 tracing with arrows marking the P waves

set2.io: Discuss related anatomy and physiology of ventricular conduction abnormalities and chamber enlargement
set2.q: A 72-year-old woman has left ventricular hypertrophy. Which axis change can it cause?
opts: Right axis deviation
Right axis deviation goes with right-sided strain, such as right ventricular hypertrophy.
Left axis deviation
Correct. The thick wall pulls the electrical vector to the left, so left ventricular hypertrophy can cause left axis deviation, with deep S waves in V1 and V2 and tall lateral R waves.
Extreme axis deviation
Extreme axis deviation is listed with ventricular rhythms, hyperkalemia and lead transposition, not left ventricular hypertrophy.
Never any change in axis
The thickened left ventricle can pull the mean vector leftward, so left axis deviation does occur, although some patients keep a normal axis.

set2.io: Discuss related anatomy and physiology of ventricular conduction abnormalities and chamber enlargement
set2.q: A 70-year-old man has a bundle branch block. Why is his QRS wide?
opts: Faster conduction down both bundles
Faster conduction would narrow the QRS. A blocked bundle forces slow cell-to-cell spread instead.
Slow myocyte-to-myocyte conduction
Correct. The blocked side must wait for myocyte-to-myocyte transmission across the heart, much slower than the conduction pathway, so the QRS widens.
A block in the atrioventricular node
A nodal block lengthens the PR interval, not the QRS. A bundle branch block widens the QRS.
Chaotic ventricular foci
Chaotic foci are ventricular fibrillation. A bundle branch block is organized conduction delayed on one side.

set2.io: Determine the electrical axis of an electrocardiogram
set2.q: A 63-year-old man has this electrocardiogram. What is his electrical axis?
opts: Normal axis
A normal axis has a mostly positive QRS in both lead I and aVF; the normal range is -30 to +90 degrees. That is not the pattern in leads I and aVF here.
Right axis deviation
Right axis deviation has lead I mostly negative and aVF mostly positive, an axis beyond +90 degrees. That is not the pattern in leads I and aVF here.
Left axis deviation
Correct. Lead I is mostly positive and aVF is mostly negative: left axis deviation.
Extreme axis deviation
Extreme axis deviation, no man's land, has both lead I and aVF mostly negative. That is not the pattern in leads I and aVF here.

set2.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with bundle branch blocks: right bundle branch block, left bundle branch block
set2.q: A 76-year-old woman has this electrocardiogram. Which conduction abnormality does it show?
opts: Right bundle branch block
Right bundle branch block puts a terminal R wave in V1 and a slurred S in the lateral leads. V1 here ends negative.
Left posterior fascicular block
Left posterior fascicular block has a narrow QRS with right axis deviation. These complexes are wide.
Left bundle branch block
Correct. Wide QRS complexes, an rS pattern in V1 whose first deflection back from the J point is negative, and notched lateral complexes without Q waves: left bundle branch block.
Right ventricular hypertrophy
Right ventricular hypertrophy shows more R wave than S wave in V1. V1 here is a deep negative complex.

set2.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with atrial enlargement
set2.q: A 67-year-old woman has these two complexes, A from lead II and B from V1, with the P wave marked. Which finding do they show?
opts: Left atrial enlargement
Correct. Panel A shows a wide, notched P in lead II, and panel B a P in V1 with a deep negative terminal part: left atrial enlargement.
Right atrial enlargement
Right atrial enlargement gives a tall peaked P in lead II and a larger positive first part in V1, the reverse of panel B.
Right ventricular hypertrophy
Right ventricular hypertrophy is a QRS finding (more R than S wave in V1). These panels mark the P wave.
Left ventricular hypertrophy
Left ventricular hypertrophy is a QRS voltage finding. These panels mark the P wave.
set2.alt: Two drawn complexes labeled A and B, an arrow over the P wave in B
